correctness.rationale: Units lift modulo the nilpotent radical J and every fiber has cardinality |J|, so unit density is computed on the Artin–Wedderburn quotient. A matrix factor in dimension at most seven can only be M_2(F_p); it costs at least the factor 1−p^−1, as does a degree-one field. This is strictly below the asserted value: with x=1/p≤1/2 the difference is x(1−x−x²+x⁴)>0. Over the perfect prime field a Wedderburn–Malcev complement exists. A sole field factor has degree dividing seven since R is a left vector space over it; the degree-seven case is commutative. With at least two field factors of degrees ≥2 and J nonzero, the degree lists (2,2), (2,3), (2,4), (3,3), (2,2,2) give radical dimensions 3,2,1,1,1 respectively. The radical dimension must be a sum of multiples of the quotient field degrees by the left module decomposition, so only (2,3) survives. Both left and right divisibility kill every Peirce component touching the cubic field. The other component has dimension one over F_{p²}, so nilpotence forces its square to vanish. Its right action is a field endomorphism, necessarily identity or Frobenius; the first gives a commutative ring, while the second yields the asserted unique ring and is visibly noncommutative. This gives the p=2 count 4·3·7=84 units and 44 nonunits. The dimension-five comparison follows from the same divisibility test, and the displayed local witness is associative because its radical has cube zero. Inspected the frozen verifier and its saved output; these check examples and a necessary profile test only, not all algebras. The argument does not rely on a fresh run of that code.

value.rationale: The fraction of units measures an intrinsic extremal property of finite algebras. The first odd dimension to exceed the elementary local bound is a natural boundary: the maximizing radical must live over the quadratic factor and a cubic field supplies the remaining dimension. The exact extremizer and rigidity explain why the transition occurs, rather than just tabulating a sample prime.
